paras: The lynching near Big Cypress Bayou was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a mob near Big Cypress Bayou in Bossier Parish, Louisiana, on Tuesday, August 14, 1888. He was accused of breaking into a store and stealing a sum of money. The report reached the national press mainly as a short addendum to dispatches about the killing of Black people by 'regulators' near Freetown.

According to a special dispatch from Shreveport to the New Orleans Picayune, 'a reliable report' had been received there that on 'Tuesday last' a Black man had been 'hanged by a mob near Big Cypress Bayou, in Bossier Parish.' The stated reason was that he had broken into a store and stolen 'a sum of money.' A separate Shreveport dispatch said only that he was 'lynched' near Cypress Bayou for stealing money 'from a store at that place.' On August 25 the St. Landry Democrat, in its Louisiana news column, placed the lynching on 'the night of the 14th inst.'
None of the reports names the man or any member of the mob, and no report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

Most white papers carried the Picayune item as the last sentence of a New Orleans dispatch reporting that more than twenty Black people had been killed by regulators near Freetown. Headlines therefore framed the story around the regulators, as in the Springfield Daily Republic's 'The Regulators at Work' and the Richmond Dispatch's 'Killed by Regulators.' The Emporia Weekly News ran the same text under a slur headline, while the Abilene Weekly Reflector and the Iola Register printed it as 'The Negro Killings' without naming the Picayune.

Other papers ran the Shreveport news on its own, the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and The Morning News under 'Lynched for Theft.' The Rock Island Daily Argus grouped it with a Florida lynching under 'Two Negroes Lynched and a White Man Shot Fatally.' The Baptist Courier of Columbia, South Carolina, folded it into its weekly review as an example of 'serious troubles' between the races in Louisiana. None of these papers added comment of its own to the brief report.
The Baptist Courier dated the hanging 'Thursday last,' but every other version of the Picayune text says Tuesday, and the Louisiana column's date of the 14th fell on a Tuesday.

reader.title: Lynching near Big Cypress Bayou, Bossier Parish (1888)
bases: Every report says an unnamed Black man was hanged or lynched by a mob near Big Cypress Bayou for an alleged store theft (A2, A8, A14).

The man was reported 'hanged by a mob' (A2) and 'lynched' (A1, A8, A14) for allegedly breaking into a store and stealing money, with no legal process mentioned; a 'mob' implies three or more, though no number is given.

Two separately worded dispatches (the Picayune special, A2, and a press dispatch, A1/A8) and a Louisiana brief (A14) agree, but all trace to Shreveport reports, and the Picayune's own text calls its source a 'reliable report' received at Shreveport rather than a firsthand account.

accounts.label: Picayune special from Shreveport
accounts.gist: A 'reliable report' received at Shreveport said that on Tuesday a negro was hanged by a mob near Big Cypress Bayou, Bossier Parish, for breaking into a store and stealing a sum of money.

accounts.label: Shreveport press dispatch
accounts.gist: A negro was lynched near (Big) Cypress Bayou on Tuesday for stealing some money from a store at that place.

accounts.label: Louisiana news brief
accounts.gist: Near Big Cypress Bayou, Bossier parish, on the night of the 14th, a negro was lynched for breaking into a store and stealing a lot of money.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Picayune item as the tail of a New Orleans dispatch on the Freetown 'regulators,' under headlines such as 'The Regulators at Work' and 'Killed by Regulators.'
Shreveport dispatches ran it as a one-sentence item headed 'Lynched for Theft' or grouped under 'Two Negroes Lynched,' with no comment.
The Emporia Weekly News reprinted the same wire text under a slur headline.

versions.value: Tuesday last (Aug. 14); 'the night of the 14th inst.'

conflicts.note: The Baptist Courier's weekly review appears to have garbled the Picayune text, which every other version gives as Tuesday; the Louisiana brief independently gives the 14th, a Tuesday.
Not a contradiction: only the Picayune text names the method.
